items.title: Data Interpretation — chart types and core operations
items.body:
DI gives data as a **table, bar graph, line graph, pie chart, radar, scatter, caselet** (worded paragraph) or a **combination** of these, and asks you to compute. The chart is just a container — the maths is always percentage, ratio, average or difference.

**The two operations that appear most**

| Operation | Formula |
|---|---|
| Percentage change | (new − old)/old × 100 |
| Share of total | part/whole × 100 |
| Average across categories | Σ values / number of categories |
| Pie slice → amount | (share% / 100) × total |
| Pie slice → angle | share% × 360° |

**Worked example (combined chart trap).** Revenue/Profit (₹ lakh): 2022 = 300/60, 2023 = 350/63. Which year has the higher *margin*? 60/300 = 20% vs 63/350 = 18%. Even though 2023's profit (63) is larger in absolute terms, **2022 has the higher margin** — 'profit as % of revenue' is a ratio, not the raw profit.

**Missing-data DI.** If a total is given, a missing entry = total − Σ(known entries).
keyPoints: Percentage change = (new − old)/old × 100 — always divide by the OLD value.
Pie: amount = (share%/100) × total; central angle = share% × 360°.
Average across categories = sum of values ÷ number of categories.
'Profit as % of revenue' is a ratio (Profit/Revenue), not the largest absolute profit.
Missing table value = grand total − sum of the known values.
'More than X' means strictly greater — exclude a value exactly equal to X.

items.title: Data Sufficiency — the 4-option convention
items.body:
You are NOT asked to find the answer — only whether the statements give **enough** information to find it uniquely. A statement is *sufficient* only if it pins exactly **one** value.

**Standard option set**

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| I | Statement I ALONE is sufficient (II is not) |
| II | Statement II ALONE is sufficient (I is not) |
| Both | BOTH together are needed (neither alone works) |
| Either | EITHER alone is sufficient |
| Neither | Even together they are insufficient |

**Method.** Test each statement in isolation first. Only if both fail alone do you combine them.

**Worked example.** *What is the two-digit number?* I: digit sum = 9 (many: 18, 27, …). II: tens − units = 3 (many: 30, 41, …). Neither alone is unique. Together: t + u = 9 and t − u = 3 ⇒ t = 6, u = 3 ⇒ **63** — unique ⇒ answer is **Both together**.

**Trap.** Do not actually solve further than needed — once uniqueness is established, stop. And 'even prime' has a unique answer (2), so a single such clue can be sufficient by itself.
keyPoints: A statement is sufficient only if it yields exactly ONE value.
Always test I alone and II alone BEFORE combining them.
'Both together' = neither alone works but the pair pins a unique answer.
The only even prime is 2, so that single clue can be sufficient alone.
You judge sufficiency, not the final numerical answer.

items.title: Permutations & Combinations — order vs selection
items.body:
The single decision that governs every counting problem: **does order matter?**

| Situation | Use | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| Arrangement, code, rank, seating in a row | Permutation | nPr = n!/(n−r)! |
| Selection, team, committee, group | Combination | nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!) |
| Seating around a round table | Circular | (n−1)! |

**Link:** nCr = nPr / r!.

**Worked example (selection).** Choose 3 players from 8: 8C3 = (8×7×6)/(3×2×1) = 56.

**Worked example (circular).** Seat 6 people round a table: fix one person to kill rotational duplicates ⇒ (6−1)! = 120. (If clockwise = anticlockwise, e.g. a bead necklace, divide again by 2.)

**Common traps.** Using nPr where the answer wants an unordered selection (over-counts by r!); forgetting to reduce circular counts by one factorial; treating a 'code/word/number' (ordered) as a selection.
keyPoints: Order matters ⇒ permutation (nPr = n!/(n−r)!); order irrelevant ⇒ combination (nCr).
nCr = nPr / r! — the two differ only by the r! ordering factor.
Circular arrangement of n = (n−1)!; divide by 2 more if clockwise = anticlockwise.
'Team / committee / group' ⇒ combination; 'code / rank / arrangement' ⇒ permutation.

items.title: Probability — formulae, dice, cards and the two rules
items.body:
**Basic:** P(event) = favourable outcomes / total equally-likely outcomes; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1.

**Standard sample spaces**

| Experiment | Total outcomes |
|---|---|
| One die | 6 |
| Two dice | 36 |
| One coin / two coins | 2 / 4 |
| A pack of cards | 52 (4 suits × 13; 4 of each rank, 13 of each suit) |

**Addition (union) rule:** P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events P(A ∩ B) = 0.

**Multiplication rule:** independent ⇒ P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B); dependent (without replacement) ⇒ P(A then B) = P(A)·P(B|A).

**Worked example (union — cards).** P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13 (subtract the king of hearts, counted twice).

**Worked example (without replacement).** Bag: 5 red, 3 blue. P(1st red, 2nd blue) = 5/8 × 3/7 = 15/56 — the denominator drops to 7 because a ball was removed.

**Balls/committee:** model as combinations — P = favourable C / total C, e.g. both red from 4R+3G = 4C2/7C2 = 6/21 = 2/7.

**Common traps.** Forgetting to subtract the overlap in the addition rule; keeping the same denominator on a without-replacement second draw; treating (2,6) and (6,2) as one outcome on two dice.
keyPoints: P(event) = favourable / total; probability lies between 0 and 1.
Two dice give 36 ordered outcomes; a pack has 52 cards (4 kings, 13 hearts, 1 both).
Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); subtract the overlap.
Without replacement: second-draw denominator shrinks by 1 — P(A then B) = P(A)·P(B|A).
Balls/committee probability = favourable combinations ÷ total combinations.
P(sum 8 with two dice) = 5/36; P(both red from 4R+3G) = 2/7.

items.title: PYQ counting & DI variants — LCM coincidence, constrained selection, handshakes-vs-hugs, %-less base
items.body:
These four UPSC CSAT patterns recur and each has a fixed method.

**LCM coincidence ('how many times together').** Periodic events with periods p, q, r coincide every **LCM(p,q,r)**; the number of coincidences in time T is **⌊T / LCM⌋**. e.g. bells at 3, 4, 6 min ⇒ LCM 12; in 72 min they meet 72/12 = 6 times.

**Constrained / dependent selection.** Count all C(n, r), then **subtract** the selections that break the dependency. e.g. pick 2 of 5 subjects where Maths-II needs Maths-I: 5C2 = 10, minus the 3 pairs of Maths-II with a non-Maths-I subject = **7**.

**Handshakes vs hugs (opposite vs same sex).** Opposite-sex pairs (handshakes) = **m × w**; same-sex pairs (hugs) = **mC2 + wC2**. e.g. 3 men, 4 women ⇒ handshakes 12, hugs 3 + 6 = 9.

**Percentage-less on a shared base.** 'Y is x% less than Z' ⇒ Y = Z(1 − x/100). To compare Y with X, use **X as the base**: (X − Y)/X × 100. e.g. X = 80, Y = 72 (of Z = 100) ⇒ Y is (8/80)×100 = **10%** less than X, not 8%.

**Common traps**
- Counting every shorter period instead of the LCM.
- Forgetting to subtract dependency-violating selections.
- Subtracting the two 'percent-less' figures directly (28 − 20) instead of re-basing on X.
keyPoints: Events with periods p,q,r coincide every LCM(p,q,r); count in time T = ⌊T/LCM⌋.
Dependent selection: count all C(n,r) then subtract the selections that violate the dependency.
Opposite-sex pairs (handshakes) = m×w; same-sex pairs (hugs) = mC2 + wC2.
'Y is x% less than Z' ⇒ Y = Z(1−x/100); compare Y vs X using X as the base.
3 men & 4 women: 12 handshakes, 9 hugs; X=80,Y=72 ⇒ Y is 10% less than X.
